shared.topic: How animals sleep differently from humans

3.5.paragraph: Animals do not all sleep the same way humans do. Most people {sl|eep} for about eight hours in one long {bl|ock} at night. Many {ani|mals} sleep in short pieces {ins|tead}. A giraffe may sleep for only a {f|ew} minutes at a time. Some bats sleep for {alm|ost} twenty hours a day. Dolphins can {re|st} one half of the brain {wh|ile} the other half stays awake. This {he|lps} them breathe and {wa|tch} for danger.

4.5.paragraph: Sleep patterns in the animal kingdom differ greatly from the human pattern of one long nightly rest. Many {spe|cies} divide their sleep into short {per|iods} spread across the day and night. Large {pl|ant}-eating animals such as giraffes sleep {on|ly} a few hours in total, {prob|ably} because lying down makes them {vulne|rable} to predators. Dolphins {so|lve} a different problem: they rest {o|ne} half of the brain at a {ti|me}, so they can {ke|ep} surfacing to breathe.

5.5.paragraph: Comparative studies reveal that the consolidated, nightly sleep of humans is far from universal among animals. Many {mam|mals} exhibit polyphasic sleep, {distri|buting} brief episodes across the {ent|ire} day. Dolphins and some {seab|irds} display unihemispheric sleep, in {wh|ich} one cerebral hemisphere {re|sts} while the other remains {al|ert}, allowing continued {brea|thing} or vigilance against predators. Researchers {attr|ibute} such variation largely to {ecolo|gical} pressures, including the risk of predation and the considerable energy demands of foraging.

shared.title: Why Roman Concrete Lasted
shared.text:
Many concrete structures built today begin to crack and crumble within a century. Yet some structures built by the ancient Romans, such as the great dome of the Pantheon in Rome and harbor walls along the Mediterranean coast, have survived for nearly two thousand years. For a long time, scientists could not fully explain why Roman concrete was so durable.

Part of the answer lies in its ingredients. Roman builders mixed lime with volcanic ash, which reacted chemically to form a strong binding material. In harbor walls, seawater slowly seeped into the concrete and reacted with the ash, producing new mineral crystals. These crystals filled tiny gaps and actually made the material stronger over time, whereas seawater gradually weakens most modern concrete.

Researchers have also found small white lumps of lime scattered throughout ancient Roman concrete. These lumps were once dismissed as signs of careless mixing, but recent studies suggest they served a purpose. When a crack forms and water enters it, the water dissolves some of the lime, which then hardens again and seals the crack. In effect, the concrete could repair itself. Today, engineers are studying these ancient techniques in the hope of designing modern concrete that lasts longer and requires fewer repairs.

shared.title: A question about a scholarship form

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: Hi, is this the financial aid office? I have a question about a scholarship application.

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: It is. Which scholarship are you applying for?

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: The academic achievement scholarship. The form says I need a recommendation letter, but I'm not sure who should write it.

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: Ideally, it should be a professor who knows your work well. A teacher from a class where you did a big project is usually a good choice.

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: Okay. What about my supervisor at my campus job? She knows me really well.

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: For this particular scholarship, the committee wants someone who can talk about your academic abilities. So a professor is better. Your supervisor could write one for the service scholarship, though.

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: Oh, I didn't know there was a service scholarship.

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: Yeah, a lot of students miss it. You can apply for both with the same online account.

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: Great. One more thing. The deadline is next Friday, but my professor said she might need two weeks to write the letter.

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: That's fine. The application itself has to be in by Friday, but recommendation letters can come in up to one week later.

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: That's a relief. I'll submit the form this week and ask her today, then.

shared.title: Holiday dining hall hours
shared.speaker: Dining Services manager
shared.text: Hi everyone, this is a quick announcement from Dining Services about the Thanksgiving break. Starting Wednesday, the main dining hall will switch to holiday hours. On Wednesday, we'll serve breakfast and lunch as usual, but we'll close at two in the afternoon, so there won't be any dinner that night. The dining hall will be completely closed Thursday and Friday. On Saturday and Sunday, we'll be open from eleven to six, serving brunch and an early dinner only. Regular hours start again on Monday morning. If you're staying on campus over the break, the convenience store in the student center will be open every day except Thursday, and it does accept meal plan dollars. Also, students who'll be here on Thursday can sign up for a free community Thanksgiving dinner at the front desk. Space is limited, so please sign up by Tuesday.

shared.question: Many parents and lawmakers are worried about how much time teenagers spend on social media. Some people believe there should be clear limits, such as age rules or daily time limits set by schools, parents, or the government. Others think teenagers should learn to manage their own use. Which approach do you think is better, and why?

posts.name: Kenji
posts.text: I think limits are necessary. Social media apps are designed to keep people scrolling, and teenagers are still developing self-control. When I was fifteen, I often stayed up past midnight on my phone and felt tired at school. A simple rule, like no phones after ten, would have helped me sleep and focus much better.

posts.name: Sofia
posts.text: I disagree with strict limits. Teenagers will eventually be adults with unlimited access, so they need to practice making good choices now. Instead of banning apps, schools should teach students how algorithms work and how to notice when they are using social media too much. Learning these skills is more useful than following a rule.
